nh_5_8_crag.blurb: A small, easy-to-reach sector of Rumney that sits close to the road and is divided into a left side and a right side. Most of the lines are bolted sport climbs, with a handful of trad lines, a couple of toprope options and a few short winter ice flows. Difficulty is broad for such a compact wall: plenty of moderate leads in the 5.7 to 5.9 range, a solid block of 5.10s and low 5.11s, and a single 5.12. That mix makes it a handy first stop for newer leaders, while stronger climbers can still find something to push on.

nh_main_area_the.blurb: The main cliff at Attitash Crag, in the Bartlett and Jackson corner of the White Mountains. It is single-pitch climbing, and the wall catches plenty of sun. Roughly two thirds of the lines are bolted sport routes, with the remainder trad. Grades start in the easy 5.4 range and build through a good supply of 5.8 and 5.9 lines into the 5.10s, with a few 5.11s and a pair of 5.12s at the top end. The trail to the base is short but steep, so expect a quieter, forested day rather than a roadside crag.

nh_03_main_slab.blurb: A wide slab on Mt. Willard above Crawford Notch, where most lines are long slab and crack routes of several pitches, up near treeline. Nearly all of the lines are long, three or four pitches, with a few shorter single-pitch variations. Difficulty is friendly: the bulk sits between about 5.6 and 5.8, with a small number of 5.9 and 5.10 lines for those wanting more. Bolt spacing on some lines is wide, so confident movement matters, and lichen can affect certain pitches. It makes a good option when the more famous nearby slabs are busy.

nh_thin_air_face.blurb: A heavily visited face on Cathedral Ledge, near North Conway, and one of the busiest trad walls in the state. The climbing is attractive face moves with comfortable belay stances and some good cracks mixed in. Every route here is traditional, with grades running from about 5.5 up to a lone 5.11; most lines fall between 5.7 and 5.10. The face is less than vertical, which helps newer multi-pitch leaders. Expect a wait for the headline line on weekends, so arrive early or have a backup plan.

nh_north_end_the.blurb: The far end of Cathedral Ledge near North Conway, known for shorter practice climbs in contrast to the long routes elsewhere on the cliff. It is mainly a trad area, largely crack climbs, with one sport line and one aid line. Grades start around 5.6 and are concentrated at 5.9 through 5.11, with a couple of 5.12s, so it suits climbers who already lead moderate cracks and want to step up. Several lines are also commonly toproped.

nh_duet_area_etc.blurb: A section of Cannon Cliff in Franconia Notch, between the Black Dike on its left and the big-wall section of the face on its right. Almost everything is trad or alpine-style, following corners, cracks and edges, and lengths run from short two-pitch lines to very long multi-pitch outings of eight pitches. Grades span about 5.5 to 5.12, with most lines between 5.7 and 5.10 and a few aid routes. Cannon is serious ground: reach the base by hiking up and traversing along the foot of the cliff, and keep an eye on weather rolling in from the west.
